evidence: AssignTaskUseCase.execute, CreateTaskUseCase.execute, MarkTaskDoneUseCase.execute and the ListTasksUseCase.execute tasks.map callback each build the same TaskDTO object literal: id, projectId, title, description, status: task.getStatus().getValue(), dueDate: task.getDueDate() ? task.getDueDate()!.toISOString() : null, assigneeId.
TaskDTO.ts declares only the TaskDTO interface. The module has no shared toTaskDTO mapper, so every task use case rebuilds the DTO itself.

CreateProjectUseCase.generateId, CreateTaskUseCase.generateId and CreateUserUseCase.generateId all use the same algorithm (prefix + "_" + Date.now() + "_" + Math.random().toString(36).substr(2, 9)), changing only the prefix: proj_, task_ or user_.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module has one clear concern: application use cases plus their DTOs for projects, tasks and users. It uses the domain repository interfaces consistently. However, it repeats rules that should each live in one place. The Task→TaskDTO mapping, including the rule that dueDate becomes an ISO string or null, is copied word for word into four use cases. TaskDTO is an interface with no mapper of its own, so each use case rebuilds the DTO by hand. The ID-generation rule (prefix + Date.now() + random base36 suffix) is also copied as a private generateId() method into three use cases, changing only the prefix. A change to either rule means editing several files, and the copies could drift apart. The rubric's duplication clause therefore fails.
